{{Short description|Recursive mathematical formula}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
In mathematics, the '''exponential factorial''' of a [[positive integer]] <math>n</math> is a quickly growing function of <math>n</math> defined by [[iterated function|iterating]] the process of [[exponentiation]], analogously to the way that the [[factorial]] can be defined by iterated [[multiplication]].

==Definition==
The exponential factorial is a positive [[integer]] <math>n</math> [[exponentiation|raised to the power]] of <math>n-1</math>, which in turn is raised to the power of <math>n-2</math>, and so on in a right-grouping manner. That is,

<math display=block>n^{\left((n - 1)^{\left(n - 2)^{\cdot^{\cdot^\cdot}}\right)}\right)}</math>

The exponential factorial can also be defined with the [[recurrence relation]]

<math display=block>a_1 = 1,\quad  a_n = n^{a_{n - 1}}.</math>

Using the recurrence relation, the first exponential factorials are:<ref>{{cite OEIS|A049384}}</ref>
{{bi|left=1.6|1=1}}
{{bi|left=1.6|1=2<sup>1</sup> = 2}}
{{bi|left=1.6|1=3<sup>2</sup> = 9}}
{{bi|left=1.6|1=4<sup>9</sup> = 262144}}
{{bi|left=1.6|1=5<sup>262144</sup> = 6206069878...8212890625 (183,231 digits)}}

==Growth rate==
The exponential factorials were introduced by Dee David Smith, in his 1974 book ''Orthogonic Taxonomy of Fundamental Concepts''. Smith used a notation for the <math>n</math>th exponential factorial that enclosed the number <math>n</math> in a three-sided box (leaving the left side open). He asked "whether or not there are other methods that give larger numbers". The answer is yes: these numbers grow quickly, but not more quickly than other known methods.<ref>{{citation|title=Mathematical Cranks|title-link=Mathematical Cranks|first=Underwood|last=Dudley|authorlink=Underwood Dudley|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1996|isbn=9780883855072|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=HqeoWPsIH6EC&pg=PA338 338]}}</ref>

The exponential factorials exhibit growth equivalent to [[tetration]] (in the sense that, for any base <math>b > e^{1/e}</math>, the exponential factorial is bounded above and below by expressions of the form <math>b \uparrow \uparrow (n + c)</math> with constant <math>c</math>). The exponential factorial of 6 (a number with approximately 5&nbsp;×&thinsp;10<sup>183&thinsp;230</sup> decimal digits) is larger than a [[googolplex]].

==Reciprocal sum==
The sum of the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocals]] of the exponential factorials from 1 onwards is the following [[transcendental number]]:
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
&\frac{1}{1}+\frac{1}{2^1}+\frac{1}{3^{2^1}}+\frac{1}{4^{3^{2^1}}}+\frac{1}{5^{4^{3^{2^1}}}}+\frac{1}{6^{5^{4^{3^{2^1}}}}}+\ldots\\
&=1.611114925808376736\underbrace{111111111111\ldots 111111111111}_{183212}272243682859\ldots
\end{align}</math>
This sum is transcendental because it is a [[Liouville number]]: its [[partial sum]]s provide a sequence of [[rational number]]s that approximate it more accurately, relative to their denominators, than would be possible for an [[algebraic number]].<ref>{{MathWorld|author=Sondow, Jonathan|id=ExponentialFactorial|title=Exponential Factorial}}</ref>
